source.title: Barycentric alignment for instance-level comparison of neural representations
source.authors: Shreya Saha; Zoe Wanying He; Meenakshi Khosla

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some tables and figure content are flattened in the web text, but the relevant results are also described in the prose.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures cross-model and cross-modal alignment using a new barycentric, orthogonal-Procrustes method rather than the original similarity method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many model-specific alignment values in Table 1 and Appendix Table 2; these are not reproduced individually here. It also reports results about stimulus consistency and human perceptual properties, but those do not directly test the claim versions. The reported correlations among stimulus-level consistency scores for different model pools are not treated as direct measures of increasing alignment with model scale.
record.test_reason: The study maps many independently trained vision models, language models, and vision plus language models into one shared space using orthogonal Procrustes barycentric alignment. It reports held-out cross-model and cross-modal retrieval and correlation. This is a different method aimed at whether representations are alignable (V4) and whether unimodal vision and language models share paired structure (V2). Appendix A.4 tests how the alignment maps depend on their training inputs (V6). It does not reproduce the Platonic Representation Hypothesis mutual k-NN measure.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that orthogonal barycentric alignment brings diverse models into a shared space, so much variation between models is reducible to symmetries. Instance-level agreement is conserved across pool constructions, shaped by training, and tracks stimulus typicality and difficulty. Post-hoc alignment of unimodal vision and language models gives near-CLIP retrieval and human-aligned image–text similarity, though CLIP stays ahead for image→text. Brain pools align stably internally but match artificial pools weakly. They acknowledge poor generalization to excluded categories.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces barycentric alignment with iterative orthogonal Procrustes transforms and evaluates instance-level consistency, cross-model retrieval, and cross-modal matching. It does not reproduce the original Platonic Representation Hypothesis measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: Instance-level scores are highly dependent on whether the test category is represented in the training inputs; category-excluded evaluation gives largely uncorrelated scores. In the cross-modal retrieval evaluation, results differ by retrieval direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Instance-level consistency scores are highly correlated across pools built in different ways. Vision: Big vs Small r=0.93, Misc1 vs Misc2 0.67, CNNs vs Transformers 0.60, Supervised vs Self-supervised 0.43. Language: Large vs Small 0.84, Misc 0.78, OpenLLaMA vs Qwen 0.58, ALBERT vs autoregressive 0.40.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The stimuli on which models converge or diverge are shared across model families and scales.

fits_no_version.finding: Consistency scores from trained vision pools are uncorrelated with those from untrained pools (r=-0.02). For language the correlation is weakly positive (r=0.22).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Stimulus-level representational agreement is produced by training rather than by architectural priors.

fits_no_version.finding: Vision consistency correlates with prototypicality (r=0.63) and rises with decision agreement (DDD), but not with human memorability, nameability or recognizability. Language consistency tracks log-probability (partial r=0.19).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-model agreement concentrates on typical, predictable inputs.

fits_no_version.finding: Consistency scores from brain (fMRI region) pools correlate weakly with those from the ResNet pool (r about 0.04–0.16), including for IT/higher-order regions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The structure of agreement in artificial model pools does not match variability between biological individuals.

record.problems: No reported sweep links alignment to model capability or performance. The cross-modal retrieval evaluation uses 200 held-out pairs, and the reported alignment transforms use 800 paired training examples. Cross-modal retrieval is asymmetric relative to CLIP. Some input-dependence results are presented as figures and qualitative descriptions rather than numerical correlations in the prose. The authors do not establish that shared training data or objectives cause the observed alignment.
record.rows_left_out: Individual model entries and their correlation, RMS, and retrieval values in Table 1 and Appendix Table 2 are not extracted separately; the paper reports many such values and the main text summarizes the alignment as strong. Other stimulus-consistency analyses, including correlations across model pools and stimulus-property associations in Sections 3.1-3.2, do not directly measure a claim version. Biological representation results in Section 3.4 are also omitted.

untested.parts: The study does not analyse alignment against model size or capability. Per-model values in Table 1 span scales but are not related to scale (see missing).

Whether cross-modal alignment rises as the vision and language models get better. Only four unimodal models are used (OpenLLaMA-7b/13b, DINOv2 ViT-L/14 and ViT-g/14), with no comparison across scale or capability.
The whole version. There are no runs of the same architecture from different seeds; the untrained-network pools are a different question.
Stitching, relative representations, and alignment without paired data. Only orthogonal maps fitted on paired stimuli are tested.
The whole version; there is no feature or circuit analysis.
Dependence on the similarity metric or its settings. Only cosine similarity and orthogonal invariance are used, with no comparison to other metrics or neighbour counts.
Whether alignment plateaus, and whether shared data or objectives explain it. The CLIP comparison is not a measure of how complete convergence between models is.

missing.what: Within-modality held-out cross-model retrieval, correlation and RMS. Summary: supervised vision pool top-1 ≥0.64 over 5,000 stimuli (chance 0.0002); homogeneous pools about 0.99; LLM pool over 300 stimuli. This is the main V4 evidence.

Per-model alignment values across scales within families would allow a V1 check, though the authors do not analyse it. They do not rise consistently with size: Qwen2.5 top-1 0.93/0.55/0.92/0.65/0.70 for 0.5–14b; ViT-T 0.64 but ViT-L 0.68 below ViT-S 0.80.
Homogeneous pools align better than heterogeneous ones (stated in the text), relevant to how alignability depends on pool composition.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V6 labels were inverted. Rows showing robustness (r8, r9, r12) count against input dependence, and rows showing degradation (r10, r11) are the V6 effect. CLIP was misused as the baseline for r1-r6; chance is the right baseline, and all retrieval values far exceed it. V7 was dropped because comparison with a contrastively trained model does not measure how complete convergence between models is. The cross-modal experiment uses only four models and small splits (800 train, 200 test) with no uncertainty reported. The paper does not test the original scaling claim despite discussing the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

versions.untested_parts: The study reports alignment across model pools containing different scales, but does not test whether alignment rises as models become larger or more capable, or relate alignment to performance.
The study measures cross-modal matching after alignment but does not test whether alignment increases as vision and language models become better.
No comparison of networks trained from different random initializations of the same architecture, or analysis of shared features or subspaces across seeds.
The study tests orthogonal Procrustes maps learned using paired training stimuli. It does not test stitching, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
No analysis of recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
The study uses cosine similarity by default and does not systematically compare similarity metrics or their settings. It does test dependence on training and evaluation inputs.

The study reports incomplete cross-modal retrieval and input-distribution dependence, but does not test whether shared training data or objectives explain alignment, or whether alignment plateaus with scale.

rows.subject: Joint universal embedding space (ViTs and LLMs)
rows.operation_detail: Applied learned model-specific barycentric alignment transforms, then evaluated text-to-image top-1 retrieval.

conditions.value: held-out test, n = 200 pairs; transforms learned using 800 training pairs

rows.note: Paired data was used to estimate alignment transforms, not to train the unimodal representations.
rows.check: CLIP is a comparator, not the baseline for the V2/V4 effect. The baseline is chance, about 0.5% top-1 over 200 pairs. Drop V7: a gap to or lead over CLIP is not a measure of how complete convergence between models is.

source_check.correct: V4: observed; V2: cannot_determine. No capability-dependent alignment trend is measured.
source_check.problem: Retrieval after alignment does not establish V2's increase with model capability.

rows.operation_detail: Compared cosine similarity between aligned image and caption projections with human compatibility ratings.
rows.note: The authors describe the result as significantly correlated with human ratings and close to CLIP.
rows.check: Fine. CLIP's tau of 0.57 is a comparator, not a baseline. The paper says significantly correlated but gives no p-value or uncertainty.

source_check.problem: Correlation with human ratings does not establish V2's capability trend.

rows.subject: Vision model pools (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared instance-level consistency scores under category-specific versus all-category training sets for the alignment transformations.
rows.measure: Correlation of instance-level consistency scores across training conditions
rows.value: Reported as highly correlated; pool-specific values are shown in Figure 3
rows.note: The prose explicitly characterizes the scores as highly correlated across these training conditions.
rows.check: The state was set against the wrong direction. V6 predicts input dependence, but the scores barely change between bird-only and all-category alignment training. Pool values are r = 0.62–0.92 (Hybrids 0.62, Supervised CNNs 0.92), readable from Figure 3. Drop V7: this concerns what the alignment maps are trained on, not shared model training data.

rows.subject: Vision model pools (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared instance-level consistency scores under category-specific versus all-category training sets for the alignment transformations.
rows.measure: Correlation of instance-level consistency scores across training conditions
rows.value: Reported as highly correlated; pool-specific values are shown in Figure 4
rows.note: The prose explicitly characterizes the scores as highly correlated across these training conditions.
rows.check: As for r8: the scores are robust to training-diet diversity. Animal pools give r = 0.50–0.91 (Figure 4). Drop V7.

rows.subject: Vision model pools (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared bird-category consistency scores when the category was included in the alignment-transform training inputs versus excluded.

conditions.value: bird-only versus non-bird images, with bird category excluded in the latter

rows.measure: Correlation of instance-level consistency scores across training conditions
rows.value: Reported as largely uncorrelated; pool-specific values are shown in Figure 5
rows.note: The authors state that scores are highly uncorrelated when the tested category is entirely absent from training.
rows.check: This is the V6 effect: scores depend on whether the test category was among the inputs used to fit the maps. Bird pools give r = 0.00–0.49 (Supervised CNNs 0.00, Misc3 0.05). The axis ranges also suggest lower absolute consistency when birds are excluded. Values are readable from Figure 5. Drop V7.

rows.subject: Vision model pools (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared animal-category consistency scores when the category was included in the alignment-transform training inputs versus excluded.

conditions.value: animal-only versus non-animal images, with animal category excluded in the latter

rows.measure: Correlation of instance-level consistency scores across training conditions
rows.value: Reported as largely uncorrelated; pool-specific values are shown in Figure 6
rows.note: The authors conclude that scores degrade substantially for categories completely excluded from the training distribution.
rows.check: This is the V6 effect. Animal pools give r = 0.03–0.43 (Self-supervised 0.03, Misc3 0.06), from Figure 6. Drop V7.

rows.subject: Vision model pools (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Applied transformations learned from ImageNet to THINGS images and compared the consistency-score similarity matrices across datasets.
rows.measure: Correlation between ImageNet- and THINGS-based score similarity matrices
rows.note: The paper describes this as strong generalization to out-of-distribution data, contrasting with the category-exclusion results.
rows.check: Pool-by-pool consistency similarity is preserved from ImageNet to THINGS (about 0.99), so there is no dataset-shift dependence here. The measure is coarse: it correlates pool-similarity matrices, not per-stimulus scores or alignment level.

relationships.condition: Four pretrained unimodal models (2 OpenLLaMA, 2 DINOv2 ViTs) jointly aligned with orthogonal maps on 800 MS-COCO pairs; tested on 200 held-out pairs and on Flickr8k-Expert
relationships.reason: Paired images and captions retrieve each other far above chance in both directions (r1-r6). Aligned image–caption similarity tracks human ratings (tau 0.54 vs CLIP 0.57; r7). The scaling part of V2 is untested.
relationships.display_finding: Image–caption retrieval exceeded chance in both directions, and aligned similarity tracked human ratings with τ = 0.54, compared with CLIP's 0.57.

relationships.condition: Orthogonal (distance-preserving) maps into a shared barycenter, fitted on paired stimuli; held-out evaluation
relationships.reason: Cross-modal retrieval is near CLIP in rows r1-r7. Based also on the text: within-modality held-out top-1 retrieval is ≥0.64 over 5,000 images for the supervised vision pool and high for the LLM pool (Table 1).
relationships.display_finding: Cross-modal retrieval approached CLIP, while held-out top-1 retrieval was at least 0.64 over 5,000 images for supervised vision models and remained high for language models.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Orthogonal (distance-preserving) maps into a shared barycenter, fitted on paired stimuli; held-out evaluation
source_check.reason: Simple orthogonal maps yield held-out cross-modal retrieval and human-aligned compatibility in r1-r7. Section 3.1 and Table 1 additionally show strong within-modality stimulus retrieval.

relationships.condition: Heterogeneous pools, or models outside the alignment maps' training categories
relationships.reason: Based on the text, not the rows: homogeneous pools reach about 0.99 top-1, while mixed pools drop to 0.64–0.87 and some LLMs (Qwen2.5-1.5b) to 0.55 (Table 1, App. Table 2). Maps fail on categories excluded from fitting (r10, r11).
relationships.display_finding: Top-1 retrieval fell from about 0.99 in homogeneous pools to 0.64–0.87 in mixed pools and 0.55 for Qwen2.5-1.5b, while maps failed on excluded categories.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Heterogeneous pools, or models outside the alignment maps' training categories
source_check.reason: Table 1 and Appendix Table 2 support reduced compatibility in heterogeneous pools, including Qwen2.5-1.5b top-1 retrieval of 0.5479. The category-exclusion results concern stimuli and consistency-score stability, not a direct measurement of retrieval failure.

relationships.condition: Test category entirely excluded from the inputs used to fit the alignment maps
relationships.reason: Consistency scores become largely uncorrelated with in-distribution fits (birds r 0.00–0.49, animals r 0.03–0.43; r10, r11). The authors say the method does not generalize to strongly out-of-distribution stimuli.
relationships.display_finding: Consistency correlated weakly with in-distribution fits for birds (r=0.00–0.49) and animals (r=0.03–0.43), indicating poor generalization to strongly out-of-distribution stimuli.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Test category entirely excluded from the inputs used to fit the alignment maps
source_check.reason: Rows r10-r11 and Appendix A.4 show fitting-input dependence: birds r=0.00–0.49 and animals r=0.03–0.43 when category-excluded and category-specific fits are compared.

relationships.condition: Category-restricted versus all-category fitting inputs, and ImageNet-fitted maps applied to THINGS
relationships.reason: Scores are largely invariant to training-diet diversity (r 0.50–0.92; r8, r9). Pool-similarity structure transfers to THINGS at about 0.99 (r12). Input dependence therefore appears only under full category exclusion.
relationships.display_finding: Scores were largely invariant to fitting-set diversity, with r=0.50–0.92, and pool-similarity structure transferred to THINGS at about 0.99; input dependence appeared under full category exclusion.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Category-restricted versus all-category fitting inputs, and ImageNet-fitted maps applied to THINGS
source_check.reason: Rows r8-r9 show substantial score correlations across category-represented fitting sets; r12 preserves pool-similarity structure at approximately 0.99. This qualifies input dependence in these tested settings; it does not establish that dependence occurs only under complete category exclusion.
